influences/christmas-date/name: The date of Christmas, Saturnalia and Sol Invictus
influences/christmas-date/sourceCulture: Roman midwinter: the Saturnalia (17–23 December) and the 'birthday of the Unconquered Sun' on 25 December
influences/christmas-date/christianForm: The feast of the Nativity of Christ on 25 December (6 January in the East and among Armenians)
influences/christmas-date/evidenceNote: The first secure evidence for a Nativity feast on 25 December is the Roman Chronograph of 354, whose list of martyrs' burials (reflecting Roman usage of c.336) begins 'VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae'. The same compilation's civil calendar marks 25 December as 'N(atalis) Invicti'. Scholars still disagree on which way the influence ran. The 'history of religions' theory says the church deliberately set Christ's birthday against the sun festival. The 'calculation' theory says Christians arrived at 25 December by their own reckoning from a 25 March conception or Passion date. Neither theory has decisive proof.
influences/christmas-date/popularClaim: Christmas is a pagan festival in disguise: the church took the Saturnalia or the birthday of Sol Invictus on 25 December and renamed it the birthday of Jesus.
influences/christmas-date/whatHistorians: Most historians accept that the date was not known from the Gospels and was fixed in Rome in the early fourth century. Hermann Usener (1889) argued that Christians deliberately replaced the Sol Invictus festival. Louis Duchesne (1889) and later Thomas Talley and Susan Roll emphasised the 'calculation' or 'integral age' hypothesis: early Christians commonly dated Christ's death to 25 March (Tertullian, Adversus Iudaeos 8), believed that the prophets died on the anniversary of their conception, and counted nine months forward to 25 December, just as Easterners reckoning from 6 April reached 6 January. Steven Hijmans has shown that no secure evidence of a public 25 December sun festival survives from before the Chronograph of 354. That makes it hard to say which feast came first, though most scholars allow that the solar symbolism was soon exploited. Saturnalia ended on 23 December and is better linked to Christmas customs such as feasting and gifts than to the date itself.
influences/christmas-date/summary: Christmas on 25 December is first attested in Rome around 336, close to a newly prominent 'birthday of the Unconquered Sun'. Whether the church chose the date to rival the sun festival or reached it by calculating from Christ's supposed conception on 25 March is a genuine and unresolved scholarly debate.
influences/christmas-date/story:
The earliest Christians did not celebrate Christ's birth at all. Their great annual feast was Pascha, and second-century writers such as Origen thought it was pagans like Pharaoh and Herod who kept birthdays. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 1.21, c.200) reports that some Christians had calculated the date of the Nativity, offering 20 May, 19 or 20 April and other dates, and that the followers of Basilides commemorated Christ's baptism in January. A passage in Hippolytus' Commentary on Daniel (4.23, c.204) gives 25 December, but some scholars think the reading may be a later interpolation.

The decisive evidence is Roman. The Chronograph of 354, a de luxe almanac produced for a Christian aristocrat by the calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus, contains a list of martyrs' commemorations (the Depositio Martyrum) beginning with Christ's birth on 25 December. Its civil calendar marks the same day 'N INVICTI CM XXX', the birthday of the Unconquered Sun with thirty chariot races. The emperor Aurelian had raised Sol to a leading place in the Roman pantheon in 274, and Constantine's coinage carried Sol Invictus until about 325. The coincidence of dates is therefore real.

From Rome the feast spread east. John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch at Christmas c.386, said it had been known there for fewer than ten years. He defended the date from Luke's chronology of Zechariah's service in the Temple. Constantinople adopted it under Gregory of Nazianzus (380), and Jerusalem and Alexandria followed in the fifth century. The Armenian Apostolic Church still keeps the Nativity together with the Theophany on 6 January. Churches using the Julian calendar keep 25 December on what is now 7 January in the civil calendar.

Christian preachers were aware of the sun festival and turned it to their own purposes. Augustine urged his hearers to keep the day 'not, like unbelievers, because of the sun, but because of him who made the sun' (Sermon 190). Leo the Great rebuked worshippers who turned to bow to the rising sun on the steps of St Peter's before entering the basilica (Sermon 27.4). Malachi 4:2's 'sun of righteousness' and the lengthening of days after the solstice became standard Christmas images. Only in the twelfth century did a Syriac commentator, glossing Dionysius bar Salibi, say outright that the church had moved the feast to 25 December because pagans kept the sun's birthday then.

The pagan-origins argument became a weapon in Protestant controversy. English Puritans abolished Christmas by parliamentary ordinance in 1647. Massachusetts fined anyone keeping it between 1659 and 1681, and Increase Mather argued in 1687 that the feast had been set to take over the Saturnalia. Scotland did not make Christmas a public holiday until 1958. Jehovah's Witnesses stopped keeping it in the late 1920s for the same reason. Today most historians present the question as open. The date's origin is disputed, but the meaning of the feast, the Incarnation, plainly comes from the Gospels and the creeds, not from Sol.
influences/christmas-date/howItHappened/: Second- and third-century Christians speculated about the date of Christ's birth without any agreed feast (Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 1.21).
A widespread belief that Christ died on 25 March (or 6 April in the East), combined with the 'integral age' idea, implied a conception on that day and a birth nine months later.
Aurelian's elevation of Sol Invictus (274) made the winter solstice a prominent public religious date in Rome.
By c.336 the Roman church listed Christ's birth on 25 December, recorded in the Chronograph of 354.
Preachers such as Augustine, Leo and Maximus of Turin took over solar imagery ('sun of righteousness') while warning against sun worship.
The feast spread to Antioch (c.376–386), Constantinople (380) and eventually most churches. The Armenians kept 6 January.
influences/christmas-date/examples/0: Chronograph of 354: 'VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae' alongside 'N INVICTI' in the civil calendar.
influences/christmas-date/examples/1: John Chrysostom's Christmas homily at Antioch (c.386) calls the feast recent there.
influences/christmas-date/examples/2: Leo the Great, Sermon 27.4, condemns Christians bowing to the sun on the steps of St Peter's.
influences/christmas-date/examples/3: The Armenian Apostolic Church's single Nativity–Theophany feast on 6 January preserves the older Eastern date.
influences/christmas-date/examples/4: The English Parliament's 1647 ordinance abolishing Christmas, Easter and Whitsun as holy days.
influences/christmas-date/defenders/0/te: Defended a 25 December Nativity tied to the 25 March conception (De Trinitate 4.5.9) and redirected solar symbolism to Christ, 'who made the sun'.
influences/christmas-date/defenders/1/te: Promoted the newly introduced feast at Antioch and argued from Luke's chronology that 25 December was historically correct.
influences/christmas-date/defenders/2/te: Preached a cycle of Christmas sermons on the Incarnation. He welcomed the feast but rebuked residual sun worship.
influences/christmas-date/critics/0/text: Increase Mather's Testimony against Several Prophane and Superstitious Customs (1687) claimed the date was chosen to take over the Saturnalia. Massachusetts banned Christmas from 1659 to 1681.
influences/christmas-date/critics/1/text: Told his Baptist congregation (1871) that he did not believe in 'the present ecclesiastical arrangement called Christmas', though he welcomed the chance to preach the Incarnation.
influences/christmas-date/critics/2/text: Have abandoned Christmas since the late 1920s as a festival of pagan origin with no biblical command.
influences/christmas-date/keptBy/0: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and most Protestant churches (25 December)
influences/christmas-date/keptBy/1: Orthodox churches on the Julian calendar (25 December Julian = 7 January civil)
influences/christmas-date/keptBy/2: Armenian Apostolic Church (6 January, with the Theophany)
influences/christmas-date/rejectedBy/0: Seventeenth-century Puritans in England, Scotland and New England
influences/christmas-date/rejectedBy/2: Some Churches of Christ, Reformed Presbyterian and Hebrew Roots groups, who reject non-biblical holy days
influences/christmas-date/calendar/pagan: Natalis Solis Invicti; Saturnalia ended 23 December; winter solstice
influences/halo-nimbus/sourceCulture: The radiate crown and luminous disc around the heads of Helios/Sol, other deities and, from the third and fourth centuries, Roman emperors
influences/halo-nimbus/christianForm: The nimbus around Christ, the Virgin, angels and saints, including the cruciform nimbus reserved for Christ and the square nimbus for living donors
influences/halo-nimbus/evidenceNote: The halo is a well-documented visual borrowing. It is absent from the earliest Christian art, appears on Christ only from the mid-fourth century, and spreads to angels, the Virgin and saints in the fifth and sixth centuries, exactly when it was standard for gods and emperors in Roman art. It was adopted as a sign of glory and holiness, not as a sign of sun worship.
influences/halo-nimbus/popularClaim: The halo is a pagan sun disc, proof that Christian saints are sun gods in disguise (a claim popularised by Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons, 1853).
influences/halo-nimbus/whatHistoriansSay: Art historians agree that the nimbus came from classical art, where Helios, Apollo, Mithras, Isis and other deities, and later emperors such as Constantine and Theodosius I, were shown with radiate crowns or discs of light. Christian artists did not use it in the third century; they took it up after Constantine, when it had become a general sign of exalted status, and gave it biblical content: the shining face of Moses (Exodus 34:29), the transfigured Christ whose face ‘shone like the sun’ (Matthew 17:2), and the righteous who ‘will shine like the sun’ (Matthew 13:43). Because emperors themselves appear nimbate in Christian churches (Justinian at San Vitale), the halo in late antiquity marked rank and sacral authority as well as personal sanctity. It is a borrowing of form whose meaning was redefined, not evidence of a solar cult.
influences/halo-nimbus/summary: The halo was borrowed from Graeco-Roman portrayals of gods and emperors in the fourth century and became Christianity’s standard sign of holiness, reinterpreted through biblical images of divine glory and light.
influences/halo-nimbus/story:
In Greek and Roman art a ring or rays of light around the head signalled divinity or heroic status. Helios and Sol wore the radiate crown; Hellenistic kings imitated it on coins; Roman emperors from Nero onwards were shown with the radiate crown on coinage, and by the late third and fourth centuries emperors were depicted with a plain disc of light, the nimbus, as a sign of their quasi-divine majesty. The same convention travelled east: Kushan kings and the Buddha of Gandharan art received haloes from the shared Hellenistic and Iranian repertoire.

The earliest Christian art, from c. 200 to the early fourth century, has no haloes at all: the Good Shepherd, Jonah and the orants of the catacombs are bare-headed. The nimbus first appears around Christ in the middle and later fourth century, in catacomb paintings such as the bust of Christ in the Catacomb of Commodilla and in apse mosaics. Over the following two centuries it was extended to angels, the Lamb, the Virgin Mary, apostles and saints. The chronology matters: Christians adopted the halo only after it had become a widely used sign of glory and rank, at a time when emperors were also routinely nimbate.

The imperial dimension is unmistakable. The silver Missorium of Theodosius (388) shows Theodosius I and his co-emperors with haloes. In the sanctuary of San Vitale in Ravenna (consecrated 547), Justinian and Theodora appear in mosaic with golden nimbi, standing near Christ, who is distinguished by a nimbus marked with a cross. Christian theology gave such imagery a precise content: the emperor’s halo indicated office and divine appointment rather than personal sanctity, while Christ’s cruciform nimbus, often inscribed with Ο ΩΝ (‘He who is’, Exodus 3:14), proclaimed his divinity.

Medieval art elaborated a code. Christ alone received the cruciform nimbus; living persons, such as Pope Paschal I in the mosaics of Santa Prassede in Rome (817–824), were given a square nimbus to distinguish them from saints in heaven; the Holy Spirit as a dove and the Lamb could also be nimbate. The Byzantine painters’ manual of Dionysius of Fourna (c. 1730) still prescribed these conventions. In the Latin West the halo shrank in the Renaissance to a thin gold ring and was sometimes abandoned for naturalistic light, a change accelerated by Protestant art, which seldom used haloes at all.

Polemical writers, from some Reformation critics of ‘popish’ images to Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853), argued that the halo exposed saint-veneration as sun worship. Modern historians of art such as Robin Jensen, André Grabar and Sabine MacCormack see a more ordinary process: Christians used the established visual vocabulary of the late Roman world to express biblical ideas of glory, and in doing so absorbed some of the imperial ideology of the age.
influences/halo-nimbus/howItHappened/0: Radiate crowns and haloes were standard attributes of solar and other deities in Hellenistic and Roman art.
influences/halo-nimbus/howItHappened/1: From the third century emperors were increasingly shown nimbate, making the nimbus a general sign of exalted status.
influences/halo-nimbus/howItHappened/2: After Constantine, Christian artists working in the same imperial visual culture gave the nimbus first to Christ, then to angels, Mary and saints.
influences/halo-nimbus/howItHappened/3: Biblical texts about shining faces and divine glory supplied a Christian rationale for the borrowed form.
influences/halo-nimbus/howItHappened/4: Byzantine and medieval convention fixed distinctions: cruciform nimbus for Christ, round for saints, square for the living.
influences/halo-nimbus/examples/0: Missorium of Theodosius I (388), Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid: emperors with nimbi.
influences/halo-nimbus/examples/1: Mosaics of Justinian and Theodora with nimbi, San Vitale, Ravenna (547).
influences/halo-nimbus/examples/2: Christ with cruciform nimbus in the apse of San Vitale and in Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna (sixth century).
influences/halo-nimbus/examples/3: Square nimbus of Pope Paschal I and of Theodora, mother of Paschal, in Santa Prassede, Rome (817–824).
influences/halo-nimbus/examples/4: Sixth-century Sinai icon of Christ Pantocrator, with a jewelled cruciform nimbus.
influences/halo-nimbus/defenders/0/text: Defended images of Christ and the saints as windows on divine glory (On the Divine Images, c. 730), providing the theology within which haloed icons were justified.
influences/halo-nimbus/defenders/1/text: His Painter’s Manual (Hermeneia, c. 1730) codified the Byzantine use of the cruciform nimbus inscribed Ο ΩΝ for Christ.
influences/halo-nimbus/critics/0/text: Oversaw the removal of images of Christ and the saints from Zurich’s churches in 1524, rejecting the visual cult of the saints as idolatry.
influences/halo-nimbus/critics/1/text: In The Two Babylons (1853; enlarged 1858) claimed the halo was a Babylonian sun symbol, a thesis rejected by historians but still widely repeated.
influences/halo-nimbus/keptBy/0: Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox iconography, where the nimbus is obligatory for Christ, the Theotokos and the saints.
influences/halo-nimbus/keptBy/2: Anglican and some Lutheran church art, especially in stained glass.
influences/halo-nimbus/rejectedBy/0: Reformed and Puritan churches, which removed images of saints altogether.
influences/halo-nimbus/rejectedBy/1: Some modern ‘pagan origins’ polemicists, following Hislop, who regard the halo as a sun-worship symbol.
